job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Chloe Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six and take the bus to a workshop on the edge of Chengdu, where Mr Gao's firm builds control cabinets for lifts. I read wiring schematics, build cabinets with Master Liu, who's sixty and has done this for forty years, and test them before they go out. I finished electrical engineering last summer with a plain pass and no internship; my final project was a motor speed controller. I share a flat with two women from the workshop and call my parents in Mianyang every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good. A job where people build things is a good job. At work I'd say nothing, because Master Liu says the loud ones finish nothing. To my friends I'd say learn a trade, not a trend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel grateful. I build and test control cabinets for lifts, and a plateau means Mr Gao keeps needing hands. I'd still owe 40,000 yuan on my loan and pay 900 yuan for my share of the flat. A steady job is what my parents wanted, and if nothing changes I can pay my loan and still send money home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning from Master Liu: reading the schematics, wiring a cabinet without a mistake, finding a fault by ear and by meter. I'd save 800 yuan a month, send 300 home, and sit the electrician's grade exam next year. I wouldn't touch AI, because I don't need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Calm. A little proud, because I'd keep doing what my hands know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch AI. What stops you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't see what it would do for me. A lift cabinet needs a person who checks every wire, because a mistake means someone is stuck between floors. I'd sooner trust my own eyes and Master Liu's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would say a girl with a trade will never go hungry, and then ask when I'm bringing someone home to meet them. My father would say nothing and be proud. They'd want me to buy a flat near them one day, and I'd want that too.

think: I'd feel **grateful**: Mr Gao keeps needing hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's up to the firms to be sensible. If software draws the schematics, fine, but they should still hire people to build and check. At work I'd keep quiet and do my share. To friends I'd say learn a skill with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the schematics and test reports might go to software, and that's maybe a third of my day. The cabinets still need building and fault-finding, so I think I'm safer than the girls in the design office. Still, Mr Gao might hire fewer new graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper into the hands-on side: apprentice harder under Master Liu, take the electrician's exam, and learn to fix the lift motors. I'd learn the software only if Mr Gao tells us to, and only what the job needs. I'd save 900 yuan a month and cut my phone plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing thunder far away. You don't know where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the software if Mr Gao asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if he asked. I don't avoid work, I avoid being the first, so if my boss Mr Gao pays for the course and sets the time, I'd go. But I wouldn't go looking for it on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about not learning it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the younger ones, who use it every day, would look better than me. In a small firm, it's easy to look slow. I'd work longer hours to make up for it, which my mother says is how my grandmother ruined her knees.

say: I'd say the firms should be **sensible**: if software draws schematics, still hire people to build and check.
To friends I'd say learn a skill with your hands.
think: Schematics and reports, about **a third** of my day, may go to software.

Save **900 yuan** a month and cut my phone plan.

fieldNote: Her resistance is to **being first**, not to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the government should slow it down or protect people. At work I'd say we should keep our hands busy and our heads down. I'd ask my parents what they think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years the schematics, testing, even the planning could go to software. I'm a plain-pass graduate who never touched AI, and a firm like ours would think twice before hiring me. The hands-on work stays until about 2031, so I'd have three years to make myself useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Master Liu to teach me everything he knows, every evening if he'd allow. I'd save 1,000 yuan a month, stop sending my parents extra, and keep my share of the flat low. If it got bad I'd go home to Mianyang and look for work in the factories near home. And I'd probably go to the temple more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It doesn't feel fair, because I did what was asked: studied, passed, took a job, and now the rule seems to have changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody exactly. It isn't one person's fault, but the companies that sell it earn money from my worry. I'd say they should pay for the people they push aside. I wouldn't shout about it; I'd write to my representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine and I have a plan, which is half true. She'd know, because she can hear it in my voice. She'd tell me to come home for New Year and eat, and I'd be glad to.

At work I'd keep my hands busy and my head down.

S2.quote: I did what was asked: studied, passed, took a job, and now the rule seems to have changed.
fieldNote: Sense of **fairness** is the core emotion: she followed the rules.
Practical plan: absorb Master Liu's skills in the 2028 to 2031 window.
Would write to her representative rather than protest.

steps.text: Ask Master Liu to teach me fault-finding every evening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, that's time to prepare. I'd say people should learn trades and firms should train apprentices, not just hire from the screen. At work I'd say nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 27, a certified electrician, with a few years of work behind me. The robots for hands-on work come around 2034, but a person with a licence and experience will still be hired to supervise. I'm hopeful but I wouldn't say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the electrician's grade exam, save 800 yuan a month, and put some towards a small flat near my parents. I'd learn the software Mr Gao brings in. I'd also think about marrying within a few years, because my parents hope I will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like an old house with creaky floors. It stands, but you listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel if the plan changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel foolish, because I like to have a plan. But my grandmother said a plan is a rope, not a cage, so I'd climb along it and keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be scrambling. With five, I'd have time to marry, to buy something, and to let Master Liu retire in peace. Five years is long enough to build one thing properly.

At work I'd say nothing new.

Even when robots arrive around 2034, someone with a licence will supervise them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time, and most people will do fine. I'd say families should look after each other and firms should train people. I'd carry on at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, with a family, a flat, and a trade that people still need. Lifts won't maintain themselves until robots come in 2039, and I'd likely be supervising them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take my exam, save 700 yuan a month and buy a small flat. I'd get married, if it's right. I might learn some of the software once it's simple and everyone uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like that picture. It looks like my mother's life, but with better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be missing from that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time with my grandmother. She is eighty-one and I see her three times a year. In ten years my grandmother may not be here, so I'd go home more now, and that's a bigger worry than any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you more willing to try new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. If everyone uses something and it's safe, I'd learn it, like I learned the phone. But I'd never be the first. I'd wait and ask Master Liu's opinion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Everything would change before my loan is paid or my parents see me settled. What would help is a firm like ours promising to keep training people, and family close by. I'd also want the government to pay for apprentices instead of handing money to people who don't work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of work, I'm afraid of being left behind through no fault of mine. My grandmother used to say that a person with a skill is never poor. I'd like to believe it still holds.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of work, I'm afraid of being left behind through no fault of mine.
portrait: **Chloe**, 22, builds and tests lift control cabinets in Chengdu under a veteran, with a plain degree and a **40,000 yuan** loan.
Traditional and market-minded, she trusts **work**, apprenticeship and family over handouts and never uses AI tools.
Her job is largely hands-on, so she feels safer than desk colleagues until about **2031**.
She is calm when little changes, anxious at two years, and most worried about **time** with family at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, which would change everything before her loan is paid or her parents see her settled.
whatWouldHelp: Her firm promising to keep **training** people.
Family nearby, and public money for **apprentices** rather than handouts.
